query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding trace amounts of Y and Hf (i.e. co‐doping) into the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature stability, creep resistance, and corrosion resistance—while maintaining a satisfactory strength–ductility balance—by stabilizing grain/phase boundaries and reinforcing the oxide scale formed during service.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast or conventionally processed AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure showing good strength and ductility but limited long-term high-temperature, creep, and corrosion performance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor addition of Y and Hf (for example, on the order of 0.5–1 wt% each) into the alloy formulation during melting/casting.
generation.conditions: Bulk-produced alloy processed under standard thermo‐mechanical treatments, then subjected to cyclic temperature fluctuations (up to ~700°C), long-term static loading (to simulate room-temperature creep), and corrosive environments (e.g., chloride-containing sulfuric acid) that mimic aerospace fastener operating conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Y and Hf are expected to segregate at grain and phase boundaries, helping to stabilize the lamellar microstructure (by impeding grain growth and phase coarsening), and to promote the formation of a more coherent and chemically protective oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: The co‐doping elements reduce diffusion rates and strengthen interfacial boundaries by forming stable sub‐nanometer segregation zones and possibly fine precipitates, which not only slows grain boundary migration (mitigating creep) but also leads to a more adherent, less spallation-prone passive film that resists high-temperature oxidation and corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped baseline, the YHf-doped alloy should display a lower creep rate under long-term load, improved resistance to thermal cycling (with reduced grain growth), and enhanced corrosion resistance (evidenced by a more stable passive film), with mechanical strength at least maintained (if not slightly increased) without substantial loss in ductility.
generation.baseline: The standard AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy produced without Y and Hf additions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected under processing conditions similar to those used in previous studies; however, excessive amounts of Y and Hf or significant deviations in processing may lead to embrittlement or undesired phase formation, limiting the applicability of the intervention.
generation.uncertainty: While recent laser cladding studies suggest that Y and Hf co‐doping can enhance thermal stability and corrosion performance in coatings, the full translation of these benefits to bulk EHEAs—especially under prolonged mechanical loading and creep conditions—remains to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of bulk alloy samples: one set of standard AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and one set with the trace addition of Y and Hf. Subject both sets to accelerated thermal cycling (repeated heating up to 700°C and cooling), long-term creep tests at room and elevated temperatures, and immersion in chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions. Characterize microstructural stability (grain/lamellae size, phase distributions) via microscopy after testing, measure mechanical properties (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, ductility, creep rate), and evaluate corrosion performance using electrochemical techniques (potentiodynamic polarization, EIS) and oxide scale adhesion.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Creep strain rate under constant load
Grain and lamellar size evolution (via SEM/TEM)
Oxide scale integrity and spallation area
Electrochemical corrosion parameters (e.g., polarization resistance, passive current density)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the YHf-doped alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvements—i.e., if its creep rate, oxide scale adherence, and electrochemical indicators of corrosion resistance are not superior to the baseline, or if ductility and/or overall strength are significantly compromised—then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively.
